analysis.one_liner: Gives Congress much broader power to block Washington, DC's local laws, regulations, and executive orders.
analysis.headline: The House Oversight Committee approved the bill 22-18 in September 2025 and reported it in January 2026; it now sits on the House calendar with no floor vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Washington, DC residents elect a local council and mayor, but Congress keeps a final check over DC laws: after the Council passes a law, Congress has a short window to vote it down. This bill doubles that review window from 30 to 60 days, and extends the check to DC executive orders and regulations, which are currently not reviewed by Congress at all. It also lets Congress strike down individual provisions of DC laws one at a time, bans the DC Council from re-passing a law Congress has disapproved, and creates fast-track procedures that make it easier for Congress to vote to nullify DC actions.
analysis.who_benefits: Members of Congress, and whatever majority holds power in Congress, gain a much larger say over how the nation's capital is governed. Any group in Congress that wants to override DC's locally elected government — on policing, elections, taxes, or anything else — gets a longer window, more targets (now including executive orders and regulations), the ability to pick off individual provisions, and fast-track procedures that limit debate to 10 hours in the Senate, making it much harder to stall a disapproval resolution.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Members of Congress and the majority party

how_it_helps.text: Extends the congressional review period for every DC law except emergency legislation from 30 days to 60 days, giving Congress twice as long to act against a DC law.
For the first time subjects DC executive orders and regulations to a 60-day congressional review, with the power to nullify them by joint resolution.
Lets Congress disapprove individual provisions of DC laws, one at a time, rather than having to reject an entire act.
Bars the DC Council from withdrawing a law once it has been sent to Congress, and from passing any substantially similar law after Congress disapproves one.
Creates expedited procedures for disapproval resolutions in both chambers, including a 10-hour debate limit in the Senate that removes the usual ability to filibuster them indefinitely.

analysis.who_pays: The roughly 700,000 residents of Washington, DC, who elect a local government but have no voting members of Congress. Their elected mayor and council would see nearly every law, rule, and order they pass subject to a longer review, with Congress able to strike down pieces of legislation and bar the Council from re-enacting anything Congress rejects.

drawbacks.text: Doubling the review period and allowing Congress to disapprove single provisions means Congress can rewrite DC policy piece by piece, repeatedly, during every review window.
Once Congress disapproves a DC law, the Council may not transmit any substantially similar act, so DC voters cannot restore a policy by re-electing a council that passes it again.
Subjecting DC executive orders and regulations to congressional review means even routine day-to-day governance in the District could be delayed or nullified from Washington.

Supporters' good-faith case is that Congress holds constitutional authority over the federal district under Article I, that the current review rules are unclear (for example, on how days are counted and whether emergency extensions escape review), and that uniform 60-day rules plus annual hearings improve accountability; the bill addresses those ambiguities while also vastly expanding congressional reach.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill does fix real ambiguities in the existing review process — it clarifies how days are counted, closes the emergency-extension loophole, and creates faster, more predictable procedures. But its main effect is a large expansion of Congress's power over a city whose residents cannot vote for the members exercising it, and the cost falls entirely on them. The oversight it adds is the kind Congress could decline to use; the burden it adds to DC self-government is permanent.

outcome.mechanism: The bill cleared the House Oversight Committee on a narrow 22-18 vote and was placed on the House calendar in January 2026, but the full House has not voted on it.

narrative.text: Rep. Paul Gosar introduced the bill on September 8, 2025, with Reps. James Comer and Harriet Hageman as original cosponsors.
The House Oversight and Government Reform Committee held a markup on September 10, 2025, and ordered the bill reported as amended by a vote of 22 to 18.
The committee reported the bill as amended on January 27, 2026 (House Report 119-463), the Rules Committee was discharged, and the bill was placed on the Union Calendar as Calendar No. 396.
No vote by the full House has occurred; the bill's latest action is being placed on the calendar, where bills await floor scheduling.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, DC residents have kept the level of self-governance they have today, because the bill has not reached a floor vote or become law. The bill's sponsors gained ground within the chamber, moving it out of committee and onto the House calendar.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: DC residents, for now; sponsors advanced it

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor is a House Republican, and the committee vote was a narrow 22-18; the sources do not publish the party breakdown of that roll call, so the partisan shape is inferred from sponsorship rather than shown directly.

industries.note: The bill gives Congress a doubled review window, power over DC executive orders and regulations for the first time, item-by-item veto power over DC laws, and fast-track procedures that make disapproval votes hard to stall. This is a direct expansion of officeholder power over a jurisdiction whose residents have no voting representation in Congress.

industries.industry: DC's locally elected government (Mayor and Council)
industries.note: The Council loses the ability to withdraw transmitted bills, to re-enact disapproved laws, and to exempt emergency extensions from review; the Mayor's executive orders and agencies' regulations become subject to congressional nullification. The local government's interest here runs alongside DC residents' interest in self-governance.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has cleared committee and sits on the Union Calendar, but placement there is no guarantee of floor time — the House leadership decides which calendar bills come up, and the vast majority never get a vote. With only four Republican sponsors and no Democratic support visible in the record, its most likely path is to sit on the calendar unless leadership chooses to schedule it.
